revision_note: Newly added with 8 verified chunks under public domain (2026-07-23, Batch 10). Source: C.A.F. Rhys Davids's 1909 translation of the Therigatha (Psalms of the Sisters), the canto entry for Maha-Pajapati Gotami, fetched directly from the sacred-texts.com etext.

content.text: Maha-Pajapati Gotami was the younger sister of Queen Maya, the Buddha's mother. When Maya died seven days after the Buddha's birth, Pajapati raised the infant prince herself, giving her own son to a wet-nurse so that she could nurse and rear the future Buddha as her own child.
content.source_name: Psalms of the Sisters (Therigatha), translated by Mrs. C. A. F. Rhys Davids (1909)

content.text: After King Suddhodana's death, Pajapati asked the Buddha to admit women to the Order. When he at first refused, she cut off her own hair, put on the yellow-brown robes, and set out on foot from Kapilavatthu to Vesali with five hundred Sakya women, arriving with feet swollen and bodies covered in dust, weeping at the gate.
content.source_name: Psalms of the Sisters (Therigatha), translated by Mrs. C. A. F. Rhys Davids (1909)

content.text: Through the intercession of the Venerable Ananda, the Buddha consented to ordain women on acceptance of eight special rules (garudhamma). Pajapati accepted them gladly, and her ordination founded the Bhikkhuni Order -- the community of Buddhist nuns.
content.source_name: Psalms of the Sisters (Therigatha), translated by Mrs. C. A. F. Rhys Davids (1909)

content.text: Once ordained, Pajapati took up meditation practice under the Buddha's guidance and, in time, attained Arahantship -- the highest fruit of the holy life, complete liberation from all defilements.
content.source_name: Psalms of the Sisters (Therigatha), translated by Mrs. C. A. F. Rhys Davids (1909)

content.text: At the Jeta Grove, the Buddha publicly declared Maha-Pajapati Gotami foremost among his nun disciples in seniority and long experience -- honoring her both as the founder of the Bhikkhuni Order and as the woman who had raised him after his mother's death.
content.source_name: Psalms of the Sisters (Therigatha), translated by Mrs. C. A. F. Rhys Davids (1909)

content.text: In her psalm, Pajapati opens with an offering of homage and gratitude to the Buddha, declaring him supreme among beings, a guide who leads all creatures out of sorrow, and expressing her own release: 'Buddha the Hero, hail! All hail to thee, / Most highest of all creatures, who didst free / Me and many mortals from all pain.'
content.source_name: Psalms of the Sisters (Therigatha), translated by Mrs. C. A. F. Rhys Davids (1909)

content.text: Pajapati's psalm closes by turning to honor her sister Maya, the Buddha's birth mother, crediting her too with a share in the fruit of the Buddha's enlightenment -- an acknowledgment of the two women together who raised him: one who bore him, and one who nursed and reared him.
content.source_name: Psalms of the Sisters (Therigatha), translated by Mrs. C. A. F. Rhys Davids (1909)
